'''''Buddleja madagascariensis''''', the '''smokebush''' or '''Madagascan butterfly bush''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the figwort [[family (botany)|family]] Scrophulariaceae. It is a substantial [[evergreen]] shrub with fragrant yellow flowers through autumn and winter.

==Description==
''Buddleja madagascariensis'' makes a sparse, lax shrub < {{convert|4|m|ft}} in height. The dark green leaves are opposite, narrowly [[leaf shape|ovate]], < 12 cm long, with [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s < 2 cm long, the surface bearing impressed [[Reticulate venation|reticulate]] [[Leaf#Venation (arrangement of the veins)|venation]], and densely pubescent. The fragrant flowers form slender terminal [[panicle]]s < {{convert|25|cm|in}} long, and range in colour from deep yellow, through orange, to pink.<ref name=Stuart/>

It is [[endemism|endemic]] to [[Madagascar]], where it grows amongst scrub on mountain slopes to elevations of {{convert|600|-|2000|m|ft}}.<ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=BUMA80 USDA] . accessed 11.11.2011</ref>

==Cultivation==
The species was first named and described by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck|Lamarck]] in 1792, and introduced to cultivation in 1827.<ref name=Hillier>Hillier & Sons. (1990). ''Hillier's Manual of Trees & Shrubs, 5th Edition.''. David & Charles, Newton Abbot.</ref> It was listed by [[William Masters (botanist)|Masters]] in his ''Hortus duroverni'' [[Canterbury]] nursery catalogue of 1831 (as ''B. heterophylla'').

''Buddleja madagascariensis'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]]. Intolerant of sub-zero (< 32 °F) temperatures, it can only reliably be grown outdoors in subtropical and tropical climate [[garden]]s, such as those of [[Southern California]] and [[Florida]] in the US, although in temperate coastal regions it can survive on south-facing walls, with added winter frost protection. Elsewhere, it is essentially a [[Conservatory (greenhouse)|conservatory]] and [[greenhouse]] plant. The shrub is grown under glass as part of the [[NCCPG]] National Collection of ''[[Buddleja]]'' held by the [[Longstock Park]] Nursery, near [[Stockbridge, Hampshire]], [[England]]. [[Hardiness zone|Hardiness]]: [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]] H2, USDA zones 9 – 10.<ref name=Stuart/>

The shrub was accorded the [[Award of Garden Merit]] by the [[Royal Horticultural Society]] (record 688) in 2002.<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web 
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/28087/i-Buddleja-madagascariensis-i/Details
|title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Buddleja madagascariensis''
| publisher = Royal Horticultural Society 
| accessdate=21 January 2018}}</ref><ref name=Stuart/>

===Naturalised species===
Popular around the world as an ornamental, ''B. madagascariensis'' has widely [[Naturalization|naturalized]] and is now classified as an [[invasive species]] in Hawaii;<ref>[http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1577&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN ISSG] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111130054647/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1577&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN |date=2011-11-30 }} accessed 11.11.2011</ref> it can also be found growing wild in southern China,<ref name=Li>Li, P. T. & Leeuwenberg, A. J. M. (1996). Loganiaceae, in Wu, Z. & Raven, P. (eds) ''Flora of China'', Vol. 15. Science Press, Beijing, and Missouri Botanical Garden Press, St. Louis, USA. {{ISBN|978-0915279371}} [http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2 online at www.efloras.org]</ref> and along the Mediterranean coast of France.<ref name = Stuart>Stuart, D. D. (2006). ''Buddlejas''. RHS Plant Collector Guide. Timber Press, Oregon. {{ISBN|978-0-88192-688-0}}</ref>

===Hybrids===
The species ''Buddleja madagascariensis'' was crossed with ''[[Buddleja asiatica]]'' to create the [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] [[cultivar]]s ''Buddleja'' 'Lewisiana' and 'Margaret Pike'.<ref name=Stuart/> It was also found to have naturally hybridized with ''[[Buddleja indica]]'' in the Grand Bassin of [[Réunion]], an island {{convert|200|km|mi}} east of Madagascar <ref name=Leeuwenberg>Leeuwenberg, A. J. M. (1979) ''The Loganiaceae of Africa XVIII Buddleja L. II, Revision of the African & Asiatic species''. H. Veenman & Zonen B. V., Nederland.</ref>
